title: Direct-Response Copywriting Fundamentals
subtitle: Learn to write words that make people act, and finish your first practice piece.
outcome: Write a clear offer, a strong hook, a persuasive structure and a clean edited draft for a real small business.
author: Built by Claude for Precious. Draft for human review.

lessons.title: What direct-response copy is
lessons.subtitle: Most writing wants to be liked. This kind wants a reply, a click or a purchase, and you can count it.
outcomes: Explain how direct-response copy differs from brand advertising
Name the one action a piece of copy is built to produce
Work out a simple response rate
lessons.body:
Every day you read hundreds of messages that want something from you. Most are noise. A few make you act: you reply, you tap the link, you send the money. The writing behind those few is called **direct-response copywriting**, and it is one of the most useful skills you can learn, because businesses pay for results they can see.

## Two kinds of advertising

Think about two ads for the same phone network.

The first is a billboard: a smiling family, a logo, the line "Connecting you to what matters." Nobody can say how many people it moved. Its job is to build a feeling over months. This is **brand advertising**.

The second is a WhatsApp broadcast: "Need data tonight? Dial \*312\# and get 5GB for ₦1,500. Valid until midnight." It asks for one specific action, it has a deadline, and the company can count exactly how many people dialled. This is **direct response**.

Both are legitimate. They do different jobs. Direct response is the one a beginner can practise on, because the feedback is fast and honest: either people acted or they did not.

:::compare
weak: Connecting you to what matters.
strong: Need data tonight? Dial \*312\# and get 5GB for ₦1,500. Valid until midnight.
note: Both examples are invented for practice. The second one gives a reader a clear action, a price and a reason to do it now.
:::

## One reader, one action

Direct-response copy is built around two things.

**One reader.** You write to a single person in a single situation, not to "everyone". A message to "all students" says nothing to anyone. A message to "a final-year student with three weeks to JAMB who keeps failing the same maths topics" reads like it was written for them.

**One action.** Every piece of copy has one job: get a reply, get a click, get a booking, get an order. If you ask for three things, most people do none.

:::keyidea
Direct-response copy is judged by what the reader does next, and you can measure it.
:::

## It started with counting

In 1923 Claude Hopkins published *Scientific Advertising*. His big argument was that advertising should be treated as salesmanship, and that you should trace results and keep what works instead of trusting opinions. Many of his ideas about testing are still the backbone of the craft a century later.

You do not need an agency to count. You need a number for how many people saw the message and a number for how many acted. Divide the second by the first.

:::example title=Work out a response rate (invented numbers)
A tailor posts an Instagram story offering a free fitting for wedding guests. **2,000 people** see it. **30 people** send a message asking to book.

30 ÷ 2,000 = 0.015, which is **1.5%**.

Next week she changes only the first line of the story and gets 2,000 views and 50 messages. That is 2.5%. Nothing else changed, so the new first line is the likely reason. That is how a copywriter learns.
:::

## Where you will meet it

Direct-response copy is everywhere once you look: sales pages and product pages, emails and WhatsApp broadcasts, Instagram and Facebook captions, paid ads, text on flyers, DMs to a prospective client, and the page for a course on a platform like Selar. If it asks a person to do one thing and you can tell whether they did, it is direct response.

## The honesty rule

Copy that persuades also carries responsibility. In Nigeria, the Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria (ARCON) oversees advertising, and the ARCON Act of 2022 requires adverts to be vetted before publication. Rules for your exact situation change, so check the current guidance before running paid adverts for a client.

The safe habit for everyone is simple: **claim only what you can prove, and never invent a testimonial or a result.** It protects the reader, protects your client, and protects you. It also works better, because specific, true claims are more believable than hype.

:::check q1-1
:::

## What you can do now

You can now tell brand advertising from direct response, name the single action a piece of copy is built to cause, and calculate a response rate. In the next lesson you will learn the part most beginners skip: finding out who you are writing to.

:::exercise title=Spot the action
Over the next two days, notice five messages that try to make you do something: an ad, a WhatsApp broadcast, a flyer, a story. For each one, write down (1) who it seems to be written for, (2) the one action it asks for, and (3) how the business could count whether it worked. Keep these notes. They become your first swipe file.
:::

lessons.title: Know the reader
lessons.subtitle: Strong copy is mostly research. The words come easily once you know who you are talking to.
outcomes: Place a reader on the five levels of awareness
Collect real customer language from public sources
lessons.body:
A beginner opens a blank page and tries to be clever. A professional opens a notebook and listens. The best line you will ever write is usually one a customer has already said out loud. Your job is to find it.

## Where is the reader in their head?

The copywriter Eugene Schwartz described five levels of awareness in his 1966 book *Breakthrough Advertising*. The idea is simple: people are at different points when they meet your message, and the same words do not work for all of them. Here are the five levels in plain language.

| Level | The reader's state | What to lead with |
|---|---|---|
| Unaware | Does not know they have a problem | A story or surprising fact that shows the problem |
| Problem aware | Feels the pain, does not know a fix exists | The pain, in their own words, and a hint it can be solved |
| Solution aware | Knows fixes exist, has not chosen | Why your way works and why others fall short |
| Product aware | Knows you, is not sure | Proof and answers to their doubts |
| Most aware | Ready to buy | The offer: price, terms, deadline |

:::example title=The same business, three readers (invented)
A solar installer in Abuja writes to three people.

To someone **unaware**: "Your fridge is costing you more than you think. Here is where the money goes each month."

To someone **problem aware**: "Fuel for the generator is eating your profit. There is another way to keep the lights on."

To someone **most aware**: "5kVA solar and inverter, installed in 3 days. Pay in two parts. Book your site visit before Friday."

One business, three different openings, because the readers are in three different places.
:::

:::keyidea
Before you write a word, decide where the reader is. The right message for a ready buyer is the wrong message for a stranger.
:::

## Use their words, not yours

Customers rarely talk like brochures. They do not say "optimise connectivity". They say "my network keeps dropping when I'm on a call". If your copy repeats their words back to them, they feel understood. If it uses your words, it sounds like an advert.

This is called collecting the **voice of the customer**. You do not need a survey. You can find it in places that are already public:

- Comments under posts and videos in your niche
- Reviews of similar products on marketplaces and app stores
- Questions people ask in public Facebook groups, X threads and forums such as Nairaland
- The questions customers ask a business on Instagram or WhatsApp, if the owner is your client and agrees to share them
- Real conversations with five people who fit the profile

**A note on privacy.** Never copy someone's name or private message into your work. You are looking for patterns in language, not stories to expose.

## A simple method

1. **Collect 20 real phrases.** Copy them exactly, including the spelling and slang.
2. **Sort them into four boxes:** pains (what hurts), desires (what they want), objections (why they hesitate), and exact words (phrases you want to reuse).
3. **Circle the repeats.** If four different people say it, it matters.
4. **Write the reader sketch** (below).

:::example title=What a sorted phrase looks like (invented)
A reader of a small-business Excel course might say: "I waste hours every month copying figures from my notebook into the computer." That sentence gives you a pain (wasted hours), an exact phrase to reuse ("copying figures from my notebook"), and a hint at what they want (to stop doing it by hand).
:::

## The reader sketch

Finish your research by writing one short paragraph about **one** person. Use this template:

> *[Who they are] is in [this situation]. They have already tried [this] but it did not work because [this]. They are afraid that [this]. What they really want is [this]. They would say it like this: "[exact phrase]".*

Keep it to one reader. If you cannot describe one person, you do not know your audience yet, and more research will help more than more writing.

:::check q2-1
:::

## What you can do now

You can place a reader on the five levels of awareness, collect real language from public sources, and turn it into a reader sketch. That sketch is the base for everything that follows. In the next lesson you will use it to build an offer and a hook.

:::exercise title=Write your first reader sketch
Pick a real small business near you (a tailor, a hair stylist, a POS agent, a tutor). Spend 30 minutes collecting 20 phrases from public sources about what their customers want or complain about. Sort them into pains, desires, objections and exact words. Then write the reader sketch paragraph using the template. Save it. You will use it in the next three lessons.
:::

lessons.title: Offers, big ideas and hooks
lessons.subtitle: A reader gives you about two seconds. The hook decides whether they spend the next ten.
outcomes: Judge whether an offer is strong
Pick one big idea for a page
Write opening lines that earn the next sentence
lessons.body:
A quick reminder before we start: the examples in this pack are invented for practice unless a source is named. They show a technique, not a real result.

## Start with the offer

An offer is what the reader gets, what it costs, and the terms around it. Copy can polish a good offer. It cannot rescue a weak one.

"Learn guitar" is a topic. "Play your first full song in 14 days, or get your money back" is an offer. It names a result, a timeframe and a reason to trust it.

:::keyidea
A strong offer names a specific result, a timeframe, and a reason to believe it.
:::

Before you write, ask four questions about the offer:

1. **What exactly does the reader get?** Name the result, not just the product.
2. **By when?** A timeframe makes a promise feel real.
3. **Why should they believe it?** Proof, a method, a guarantee, or a sample.
4. **What does it cost, and what is the risk?** State the price plainly. If you can honestly reduce the risk, with a refund or a free sample, do.

If you cannot answer all four, fix the offer before touching the headline. A beautiful hook on a vague offer only gets more people to see something unconvincing.

## Choose one big idea

The big idea is the single angle that makes the offer feel new. A meal-prep service could sell saved time, saved money or better eating. Pick one and let everything else support it. A page that argues for all three convinces no one of any.

A quick test for a big idea: **could a competitor put their name on it and say the same thing?** If yes, it is not yet an idea, it is a category. "Fresh, quality food" fits every kitchen. "Dinner for the week, cooked in your free Sunday hour" belongs to one business.

## Write hooks that earn the next sentence

A hook has one job: make the next line worth reading. This matters because people skim. In a well-known 1997 test, Jakob Nielsen found that most users scanned new web pages and only a small share read word by word. A page does not get read until the opening earns it.

The advertising writer David Ogilvy, in *Confessions of an Advertising Man*, made a similar point: far more people read the headline than the text beneath it, so the headline carries most of the work. That was an observation from his own era, not a law, but it is a good reason to spend real time on your first line.

Four patterns work again and again:

- **A specific number.** "7 mistakes that stop new freelancers getting a second client."
- **A sharp question.** "Still paying for data that finishes before the week does?"
- **A surprising claim.** "Your phone is not the reason you cannot focus."
- **The start of a story.** "I was about to close my shop when a customer asked one question."

:::compare
weak: Tips for better sleep
strong: The 3-minute habit that ended my 2 a.m. wake-ups
note: The strong version has a number, a time and the start of a story. Each one gives the reader a reason to keep going.
:::

### Match the hook to the reader

Remember the five levels of awareness from the last lesson. A hook for someone who is *most aware* can be an offer: "Book before Friday and save ₦5,000." A hook for someone who is *unaware* must first show them the problem. Reach for your reader sketch before you pick a pattern.

### Write ten, then choose one

Never settle for your first hook. Write ten for the same offer, mix the four patterns, and then read them aloud. Cross out the vague ones. Choose the one that is specific and true. The other nine often become the subject lines, captions and ad variations you test later.

:::check q3-1
:::

:::exercise title=Offer, idea, ten hooks
Use the reader sketch from Lesson 2. (1) Write the offer in one sentence answering the four questions. (2) Write your big idea in one line, then run the competitor test. (3) Write ten hooks using all four patterns. (4) Circle your best two and say why. If you cannot say why, they are not ready yet.
:::

lessons.title: Structure that persuades
lessons.subtitle: A hook gets attention. Structure carries the reader from interest to action without losing them.
outcomes: Use AIDA and PAS as checklists
Write a clear, low-friction call to action
lessons.body:
You have a reader, an offer and a hook. Now you need a path: a way to take a busy reader from "maybe" to "yes" without confusing them. Writers use frameworks for this. Treat them as checklists, not magic formulas. They remind you of the steps a reader needs.

## AIDA: the classic path

AIDA stands for **Attention, Interest, Desire, Action**. It is usually credited to E. St. Elmo Lewis, an American advertising man writing in the early 1900s, though historians note that the idea appeared in pieces and was not a neat model from day one.

- **Attention:** the hook.
- **Interest:** show you understand the reader's situation.
- **Desire:** show the result they want, with proof.
- **Action:** tell them the single next step.

If a draft feels flat, check which step is missing. Most weak copy has attention and action but skips the middle.

## PAS: problem, agitate, solve

PAS is a widely taught formula for readers who feel a problem. It has three steps.

1. **Problem:** name the pain in the reader's own words.
2. **Agitate:** show what it costs if nothing changes, without exaggerating.
3. **Solution:** present your offer as the way out.

:::example title=One offer, written with PAS (invented)
*Offer: a 30-day Excel course for small shop owners, sold online.*

**Problem:** You close the shop tired, then spend an hour copying figures from your notebook into the computer.

**Agitate:** One wrong number and you do not know whether you made money this month. Hours disappear that you could spend with customers or at home.

**Solution:** In 30 days, learn the exact five Excel tricks that turn your notebook into a sales sheet you can finish in ten minutes. Start with the free first lesson below.
:::

Notice what the agitate step is not: it is not a threat and it does not invent fear. It points at a real cost the reader already feels.

:::keyidea
Every persuasive piece answers the reader's silent questions in order: Is this for me? Is it believable? What do I do next?
:::

## Bullets that make people want more

Bullet lists are some of the most-read parts of a page. A good bullet joins a **benefit** with a hint of **curiosity**, and does not give everything away.

:::compare
weak: Learn about Excel formulas
strong: The 3-minute formula that finds a missing ₦12,500 in your monthly sales sheet
note: The strong bullet promises something specific and leaves a reason to read on. Only write a bullet like this if your lesson truly delivers it.
:::

Three rules for bullets: start with the benefit, be specific, and keep each one to a single line when you can.

## Proof

Readers do not take your word for it. Proof comes in many forms: a real customer story with a real result, a screenshot with permission, a clear guarantee, a free sample, or a simple explanation of how your method works. **Use only true proof.** If you have none yet, say so honestly and offer a small risk-free step instead. An invented testimonial is not a shortcut, it is a lie that can end a business and break advertising rules.

## The call to action

The call to action (CTA) tells the reader what to do now. Good CTAs are specific, easy, and say what happens next.

- Weak: "Click here."
- Better: "Send the word SHEET on WhatsApp and get the free first lesson in two minutes."

Keep one main action. If you must offer a second, make it clearly smaller (for example "or see the price list"). Reduce effort wherever you can: fewer fields, fewer steps, a button where the reader already is.

## How long should it be?

There is no ideal length. The rule of thumb: **the higher the price and the more doubt the reader has, the more you need to say.** A ₦500 data offer to a ready buyer can be two lines. A ₦150,000 course to someone who has never heard of you needs the full path: problem, proof, answers to doubts, a guarantee and a clear next step. Write as much as the reader needs to say yes, and not one sentence more.

:::check q4-1
:::

:::exercise title=Write it two ways
Take the offer from Lesson 3. Write a 120 to 180 word message in PAS form. Then rewrite the opening and middle in AIDA order and see which step feels weaker. Add three curiosity bullets and one clear CTA. Keep both versions in your notes.
:::

lessons.title: Edit and ship
lessons.subtitle: The draft is where you find the idea. The edit is where you earn the result.
outcomes: Edit a draft in focused passes
Plan a simple, fair test of two versions
Finish and publish a first practice piece honestly
lessons.body:
Nobody writes good copy in one pass. Professionals write a rough draft quickly, then edit in several short passes, each with one question. This lesson gives you those passes and then shows you how to finish and test your work.

## Edit in passes

Do each pass separately. Trying to fix everything at once means you fix nothing.

1. **The "so what?" pass.** Read every sentence and ask: so what does this do for the reader? Cut or rewrite what does nothing.
2. **The "prove it" pass.** Circle every claim. Is there proof, a number or an example? If not, add it, soften the claim, or remove it.
3. **The specifics pass.** Replace vague words ("quality", "best", "amazing") with a detail the reader can picture.
4. **The reader's-words pass.** Swap your jargon for the phrases from your research.
5. **The cut pass.** Remove a quarter of the words. Delete "very", "really", "just", and any sentence that repeats another.
6. **The read-aloud pass.** Read it out loud. Where you stumble, the reader will stumble. Shorten that sentence.
7. **The action pass.** Is there one clear action? Can the reader do it in one step?

:::keyidea
Good copy is rewritten, not discovered. Edit in single-question passes, and cut until every line earns its place.
:::

:::compare
weak: We offer high-quality, affordable tailoring services for all your needs.
strong: Your agbada, ready in 5 days and fitted twice, from ₦45,000. Book a free fitting this week.
note: The strong version names a product, a time, a price and an action. The weak one could describe any tailor.
:::

## The final checklist

Before you publish, check every item:

- One reader, described in your sketch
- One offer: result, timeframe, proof, price and risk
- A hook that is specific and true
- A clear path: attention, interest, desire, action
- Every claim has proof or is softened
- No invented testimonials or results
- One main call to action
- Read aloud and trimmed

## Test fairly

A test compares two versions to see which gets a better response. A few rules keep you honest:

- **Change one thing at a time.** If you change the hook and the price, you will not know which mattered.
- **Show both versions to similar audiences at similar times.**
- **Wait for enough responses.** Three clicks versus five clicks tells you almost nothing. Real results need a decent number of responses before you trust a pattern.
- **Keep a log.** Write down the version, the date, the audience and the result. Over time the log becomes your own rulebook.

## Ship your first spec piece

A **spec piece** is a sample you write without being paid, to practise and to show your skill. It is a good first portfolio item. Do it properly:

- Choose a real small business or product.
- Use public information, and ask permission if you plan to show it as work for that business.
- **Label it clearly as a practice sample.** Never present it as real client work or invent results it supposedly achieved.
- Aim for 150 to 250 words: a hook, a short body, proof you can honestly use or none, and one call to action.

:::check q5-1
:::

:::exercise title=Your first practice piece
Using your reader sketch, offer, big idea and hooks, write a 150 to 250 word message (a WhatsApp broadcast, an Instagram caption or a short email) for your chosen business. Run the seven editing passes. Then run the checklist. Save it as a spec piece labelled "Practice sample". If you have permission, share it with the business and ask for one honest reaction.
:::

## You have finished the pack

You can now research a reader, shape an offer, write hooks, structure a message, edit it, and test it fairly. That is a complete loop, and the real learning comes from repeating it. Write one piece every week, log what you learn, and keep a swipe file of work that makes you act.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is a direct-response message?

options.text: A billboard with a logo and the line “Trusted by families everywhere”
A WhatsApp broadcast: “Order by 5 pm today and get delivery in Lagos tomorrow”
A company anniversary video with music
A shop sign showing the shop's name

quiz.explanation: The second asks for one specific action, gives a deadline, and the business can count the orders. The others build awareness but do not ask for a measurable action.

quiz.prompt: A story is seen by 4,000 people and 80 of them reply to book. What is the response rate?
quiz.explanation: 80 ÷ 4,000 = 0.02, which is 2%. Divide the number who acted by the number who saw it.

quiz.prompt: How many main actions should one piece of direct-response copy ask for?

options.text: As many as possible, to give people choices
Three, so there is always one they like

quiz.explanation: Asking for several things at once leaves most people doing none. One reader, one action.

quiz.prompt: Which habit is the safest when writing persuasive copy?

options.text: Invent a testimonial if you do not have one yet
Claim only what you can prove
Exaggerate results so you stand out
Hide the price so people ask

quiz.explanation: Claims you can prove protect the reader, your client and you. Invented results are dishonest and can break advertising rules.

quiz.prompt: A reader knows they have a problem but does not know that a fix exists. Which level of awareness is this?
quiz.explanation: Problem aware readers feel the pain. Lead with the pain in their own words and hint that it can be solved.

quiz.prompt: Where is the best place to find the exact words customers use?

options.text: Public comments, reviews, questions and real conversations

quiz.explanation: Real customer language lives in comments, reviews, forum questions and conversations. Copy phrases, not private details.

quiz.prompt: What is a reader sketch?

options.text: A short paragraph about one specific reader: situation, past attempts, fears, wants and exact words
A list of every person who might buy

quiz.explanation: It keeps you writing to one real person instead of “everyone”.

quiz.prompt: Which phrase better reflects the voice of the customer?

options.text: My network keeps dropping when I am on a call

quiz.explanation: Customers describe problems in plain, specific language. Repeating their words makes them feel understood.

quiz.prompt: Which opening is the strongest hook?

options.text: Great ways to save money on food
How one family cut their food bill by ₦38,000 in 30 days

quiz.explanation: The second names a result, an amount and a timeframe, and it hints at a real story. The others are broad promises with nothing to check.

quiz.prompt: Which of these is an offer rather than a topic?

options.text: Play your first full song in 14 days, or get your money back

quiz.explanation: An offer names a result, a timeframe and a reason to trust it.

quiz.prompt: You have a hook but the offer is vague. What should you do first?
quiz.explanation: A strong hook on a weak offer sends more people to something unconvincing. Fix the offer, then write the hook.

quiz.prompt: What is a good test for a big idea?

options.text: A competitor could not put their name on it and say the same thing
It has three benefits in one line

quiz.explanation: If anyone could say it, it is a category, not an idea.

quiz.prompt: In the AIDA path, which step usually gets skipped in weak copy?
quiz.explanation: Weak copy often has a hook and a button but skips the middle, where understanding and proof are built.

quiz.prompt: What does the “agitate” step in PAS do?

options.text: Shows the real cost of leaving the problem unsolved, without exaggerating

quiz.explanation: Agitating points at a real cost the reader already feels. It is not a threat and does not invent fear.

quiz.prompt: Which bullet is the strongest?

options.text: The 3-minute formula that finds a missing ₦12,500 in your monthly sales sheet

quiz.explanation: It joins a specific benefit with curiosity. Only write it if the lesson delivers it.

quiz.prompt: A ₦150,000 course sold to strangers compared with a ₦500 data offer to ready buyers usually needs...

options.text: More copy, because the price and doubt are higher

quiz.explanation: The higher the price and the more doubt, the more the reader needs to hear before saying yes.

quiz.prompt: You are testing two headlines. Version A got 3 clicks and version B got 5. What is the sensible conclusion?

options.text: B is clearly better, use it forever
There are too few responses to be sure, keep testing
Tests do not work in Nigeria

quiz.explanation: Small numbers swing by chance. Wait for enough responses before trusting a pattern.

quiz.prompt: What does the “prove it” editing pass look for?

options.text: Claims with no proof, number or example

quiz.explanation: Circle every claim, then add proof, soften it or remove it.

quiz.prompt: How should a spec piece be shown in a portfolio?

options.text: As real client work with invented results
Clearly labelled as a practice sample
As a screenshot of someone else's ad

quiz.explanation: Labelling it honestly keeps your portfolio trustworthy. Never invent results or claim client work you did not do.

quiz.prompt: When running a test, how many things should you change at once?

options.text: Everything, to get a big difference
One, so you know what caused the change

quiz.explanation: Changing one thing lets you connect the result to the cause.

# Sources and credits

Everything in this pack is written in original words. Ideas are credited here so you can read the originals. Examples are invented for practice unless stated.

## Checked against a named source

- **Jakob Nielsen, "How Users Read on the Web", Nielsen Norman Group, 30 September 1997.** In the test described, 79% of users scanned any new page and 16% read word by word. This is an old study. Treat it as a reminder that people skim, not a law. https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-users-read-on-the-web/
- **E. St. Elmo Lewis and AIDA.** Edward K. Strong Jr. (1925) credits Lewis with the "attract attention, maintain interest, create desire" idea from 1898, with "get action" added later. Historians note the idea appeared in scattered pieces in Lewis's writing and was not a single formal model at first. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E._St._Elmo_Lewis
- **Eugene Schwartz, *Breakthrough Advertising* (1966).** The five levels of awareness (unaware, problem aware, solution aware, product aware, most aware). Summarised in the pack in original words. Summary used for checking: https://selzee.com/eugene-schwartz-5-levels-of-awareness
- **Advertising Regulatory Council of Nigeria (ARCON).** The ARCON Act 2022 requires adverts to be vetted before publication and provides penalties for offences. Rules change, so check current guidance before running paid adverts. https://advertcouncil.gov.ng and an overview at https://www.mondaq.com/nigeria/advertising-marketing--branding/1290290/an-overview-of-the-advertising-regulatory-council-of-nigeria-act-2022

## Cited from well-known books, not independently re-checked
